excerpt: TAP Air Portugal used to let golfers check clubs for free — that blanket promotion is gone. Here's what determines whether you pay now, and roughly how much.

content.text: TAP Air Portugal isn't the airline most golfers fly direct into Faro on — its own Faro routes are limited to Lisbon and Funchal — but plenty of travellers connecting through Lisbon from further afield, or combining a few days in the capital with a golf trip to the Algarve, end up flying TAP with their clubs. If you're one of them, it's worth knowing the rules changed: TAP used to let golfers check clubs for free as a standing promotion, and that's no longer guaranteed by default.
How TAP treats golf clubs

Golf equipment travels as checked baggage, and TAP treats a golf bag as **one single item** regardless of its actual shape, with combined dimensions (length + width + height) up to **158cm** and a weight limit of **32kg**. Kept within those limits, no oversize or out-of-gauge surcharge applies on top of whatever else you owe.
When it's included in your fare

TAP's own baggage terms say sports equipment can be included in your free hold baggage allowance if it fits the limits above — so the first question is what your fare already includes. **Basic and Classic** fares typically come with one free checked bag up to 23kg, **Plus** fares with two, and **Business class** allows up to 32kg. If your golf bag is the only hold item you're checking and it's under your fare's weight limit, it can use that included allowance rather than costing anything extra.
When you'll pay, and roughly how much

Where TAP has changed is that the golf-specific free-transport promotion it used to run is gone, so if your clubs go beyond what your fare already covers — a Basic fare with no included bag, or a golf bag on top of a separate suitcase — you're charged TAP's sports equipment fee rather than getting any golf-specific discount. On European routes (which covers a Lisbon–Faro connection), that runs from roughly **€45 booked online**, more if paid at the airport, and considerably more again on intercontinental sectors. Treat that as a starting point rather than a fixed number — TAP prices it by route and how far ahead you book, so check the actual figure in Manage My Booking for your specific flights.
How to book it

Sports equipment can be added when you book, through Manage My Booking, at check-in, at an airport kiosk, or via the TAP Contact Centre — up to 24 hours before departure, though it's subject to availability, so earlier is safer than leaving it to the last day. It can also be paid for using TAP Miles&Go points instead of cash, worth checking if you fly TAP often enough to have a balance sitting there.
The alternative: skip the connection hassle and rent at Faro

If your TAP itinerary already involves a connection through Lisbon, adding a golf bag into that mix — checking it through, hoping it makes a tight transfer, collecting it at the other end — is its own source of stress even before fees come into it. Renting on arrival sidesteps the whole thing. Two operators are based directly at **Faro Airport (FAO)**, one in the arrivals hall and one at a departures-terminal counter, so you can walk off your final flight and either take a set with you or have it delivered to your hotel or first round.

Rates, pickup points and delivery areas differ between providers, so it's worth a quick comparison — see our [guide to club rental across the Algarve](/shops) for the full picture beyond just these two.
Bottom line

Flying TAP with your own clubs can still be free if your fare includes a bag and your golf set fits inside that allowance — but don't assume it, since the old blanket golf promotion is gone. Check what your specific fare includes before you fly, and if a Lisbon connection makes the logistics feel like more trouble than it's worth, renting locally once you land in Faro is a straightforward way around it.

excerpt: A month-by-month guide to the golf season in the Algarve: course crowds, green fees, hotel prices, temperatures, daylight and rain, plus the best months to play.

content.text: Golf in the Algarve is a year-round sport. The courses never shut for a season the way they do in northern Europe, and you can tee off in shorts in January nearly as easily as in July. But the golf season in the Algarve still has a rhythm: green fees at many courses are a third or more lower in the cheapest months than at peak, hotels fill and empty with the beach crowd rather than the golf crowd, and the weather shifts from warm-and-dry to short-and-showery and back again. This month-by-month guide covers what to expect on the course, in your hotel and in your wallet across the whole year, then names the months that give you the best balance.

Two patterns are worth holding in mind before the detail. First, green fees peak in spring and autumn (roughly March to May and October) and bottom out in mid-summer and mid-winter. Pestana's published rates, for example, run about €95 in the low season against €180 at peak for its Carvoeiro courses. Second, hotel prices and crowds follow the opposite curve: they are highest in July and August, when Algarve golf is actually at its quietest, and lowest from November to February, when some resort hotels cut back service or close for a few weeks.
Playing golf in the Algarve in January

January is the quietest and cheapest month of the year. Fairways can be soft after winter rain and a handful of courses take a short maintenance break, but tee sheets are wide open and you can often walk on. Green fees are at their lowest, and rooms are cheap where hotels are open, though choice is limited because some resorts stay closed until February. Days are short, so book a late-morning tee time and you will still finish comfortably before dark. Bright, still mornings are common, and the rain that does come tends to arrive in bands of a day or two rather than constant drizzle.
**Quick numbers:** highs around 16°C, lows around 8°C. About 10 hours of daylight. About six rainy days and 49 mm of rain. Read the full [January guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-january).
Playing golf in the Algarve in February

February is still low season for green fees on most courses, but conditions start to turn. Rainfall eases, the daylight lengthens noticeably and the almond blossom is out. Courses get busy only around the UK half-term week, when families arrive; outside that week you will find space and value. More hotels reopen than in January, widening your choice. This is one of the best-value windows of the year, as long as you accept that an afternoon shower is still possible and the greens are not yet at their spring pace.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 17°C, lows around 9°C. About 11 hours of daylight. About five rainy days and 42 mm of rain, the driest month of the winter. Read the full [February guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-february).
Playing golf in the Algarve in March

In March the season steps up. Courses fill out as spring golf packages begin and Easter approaches, and green fees move into the peak band on many courses. The trade-off is some of the year's best playing weather: warm afternoons, long-enough days and grass growing back into the fairways. Hotels raise their rates but are not yet full. Book tee times and rooms well ahead for the Easter fortnight, which is the single busiest stretch of spring.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 19°C, lows around 11°C. About 12 hours of daylight. About six rainy days and 47 mm of rain, usually in short spells. Read the full [March guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-march).
Playing golf in the Algarve in April

April is peak season in full swing and, for many golfers, the best all-round month to play. Days are long, afternoons are reliably warm without being hot, the rough is green and the courses are in excellent shape. It is also one of the busiest and most expensive months: green fees are at or near their annual high, popular courses book out days ahead and hotel rates are firm. If April is your window, reserve everything early and consider the quieter east or west ends of the region.
**Quick numbers:** highs around 21°C, lows around 12°C. About 13 hours of daylight. About five rainy days and 39 mm of rain. Read the full [April guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-april).
Playing golf in the Algarve in May

May is arguably the peak of the golf calendar. The weather is close to ideal, dry and warm with a very low rain risk, and the courses are busy, with green fees at or near their spring peak. Hotels are busy, but the school-holiday surge has not yet arrived, so rooms are easier to find than in July. Book tee times ahead, and aim for morning slots as the days warm up.
**Quick numbers:** highs around 23–24°C, lows around 15°C. About 14 hours of daylight. About four rainy days and 26 mm of rain. Read the full [May guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-may).
Playing golf in the Algarve in June

June is the pivot month. Green fees drop back into the low-season band as the heat builds, yet the golf is still very good if you tee off early, and course traffic thins through the month. Hotels move the other way, climbing toward their summer peak as the beach season opens and the first school holidays begin, so you may pay less for golf and more for your room than you would in April. Daylight is at its maximum, which makes early and twilight tee times genuinely comfortable. The west of the region is noticeably cooler than the centre and east from June onwards.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 27°C, lows around 18°C. Nearly 15 hours of daylight, the longest of the year. Usually no more than one rainy day, and about five days above 30°C in Faro. Read the full [June guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-june).
Playing golf in the Algarve in July

July is hot, dry and quiet on the course. Along with mid-winter, July and August are the cheapest months for green fees, and tee sheets stay open because most visitors are on the beach rather than the fairway. Play at dawn or from late afternoon; the middle of the day is uncomfortable and hard on your scorecard. Hotels are the opposite story, full and expensive with UK, Irish and Portuguese school holidays all overlapping. Book accommodation months ahead, then enjoy the pick of tee times once you arrive. It runs hotter inland, around [Silves](/courses/silves) for example, and cooler in the far west.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 29°C, lows around 20°C, with about 13 days above 30°C in Faro. About 14.5 hours of daylight. Effectively no rain. The far west is cooler, at around 25°C. Read the full [July guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-july).
Playing golf in the Algarve in August

August is much like July: low green fees, quiet courses, packed and pricey hotels. The heat is the main obstacle, so this is a month for buggies, early alarms and plenty of water. Courses are well irrigated and stay green, though summer greens are slower than spring ones. If you can find a room at a sensible price, August is a cheap month to play a lot of golf around a family beach holiday.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 29°C, lows around 20°C, with about 12 days above 30°C in Faro. About 13.5 hours of daylight. Almost no rain. The far west is cooler, at around 26°C. Read the full [August guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-august).
Playing golf in the Algarve in September

For many golfers September is the best month of all. The extreme heat fades, the sea is at its warmest, rain is still rare and the beach crowds thin once UK schools go back at the start of the month. Green fees climb back towards their autumn peak, and hotel rates ease from their August peak. Early September gives you summer weather at shoulder prices; late September gives you near-perfect golfing conditions as the peak autumn window opens.
**Quick numbers:** highs around 26°C, lows around 18°C. About 12.5 hours of daylight. About two rainy days and 22 mm of rain. Read the full [September guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-september).
Playing golf in the Algarve in October

October is the autumn peak. Courses are extremely busy and green fees are at or close to their annual high as northern Europe escapes the cold. The weather is usually excellent early in the month, still warm and mostly dry, though the first serious rain of the season can arrive. Some courses overseed their fairways now, which can mean temporary greens or minor disruption. Book tee times and hotels as far ahead as you can, because October sells out early.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 23°C, lows around 16°C. About 11 hours of daylight, dropping fast once the clocks go back at the end of the month. About six rainy days and 56 mm of rain. Read the full [October guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-october).
Playing golf in the Algarve in November

In November the season winds down. Green fees fall back to mid-season on most courses, and lower still late in the month, and the courses are quiet again. Weather is the gamble: you can get a run of warm, calm, blue-sky days or a week of Atlantic fronts, and November is statistically one of the wettest months. Fairways soften. Hotels are cheap and some begin to close for winter. Good value for flexible golfers who will take the weather as it comes.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 20°C, lows around 12°C. About 10 hours of daylight. About seven rainy days and 76 mm of rain, and in the far west November is the wettest month of the year. Read the full [November guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-november).
Playing golf in the Algarve in December

Along with January, December is the quietest and cheapest month. Green fees are at their lowest, courses are near empty and you can often book same-day. It is also the wettest month on average and the darkest, with under 10 hours of daylight, so tee times cluster around the middle of the day. A few courses close briefly for maintenance and some hotels shut until February, though the Christmas and New Year week is a small exception, with a short spike in demand and prices.

**Quick numbers:** highs around 17°C, lows around 10°C. About 9.5 hours of daylight, the shortest of the year. About seven rainy days and 90 mm of rain, the most of any month in Faro. Read the full [December guide](/guide/algarve-golf-in-december).
The best months to play golf in the Algarve

If you want the best conditions and don't mind paying for them, play from late April into May or from late September into October. You get long days, warm and dry weather and courses in top shape, against the highest green fees of the year, the fullest tee sheets and firm hotel rates. Book months ahead.

For the best value with still-reliable weather, look at June, November or late January into February. Green fees are noticeably below their peak, the courses are quieter and the weather is usually good enough, with the trade-offs of summer heat in June, a real chance of rain in November and short days in winter.

For the cheapest golf, play in June, July or August. Green fees are as low as they get and the courses are quiet, but you have to tee off early to beat the heat and you will pay peak prices for a busy hotel. Mid-winter, December and January, is just as cheap for both golf and rooms, with the trade-off of short days, soft fairways and the highest rain risk of the year.

In short: spring and autumn for conditions, winter for a bargain, high summer for empty fairways if you can handle the heat. The quietest tee sheets of all are in December, January, July and August. When you have picked your month, you can compare courses, green fees and nearby hotels on the [interactive map](/).
**Fancy a competition?** See our guide to [golf tournaments in the Algarve](/guide/golf-tournaments-in-the-algarve), with amateur events you can enter from December to May.

**Staying for the winter?** Our guide to [long-stay golf in the Algarve](/guide/long-stay-golf-in-the-algarve) compares short-term memberships, round packages and golf societies, and explains how long EU and UK visitors can stay.

excerpt: Wizz Air prices golf clubs dynamically, so the fee can vary a lot by route and how early you book. Here's what drives the price and how to avoid the higher end.

content.text: Wizz Air flies into Faro from both London Gatwick and Luton, alongside its wider Central and Eastern European network, so it's a genuine option for UK golfers as well as anyone connecting through the airline's other bases. One thing to know before you rely on a number you found online: Wizz Air prices almost everything dynamically, sports equipment included, so the fee for your golf clubs can shift more than it does with most other airlines on this list.
How Wizz Air classifies golf clubs

Golf clubs go under **sports equipment**, and Wizz Air is explicit that this doesn't count toward your normal checked baggage allowance — it's a separate item you book and pay for on its own. The airline also asks that clubs be packed in a proper protective bag or pouch rather than loose or wrapped in something improvised, since that's what gets handed to baggage handlers for the hold.
Weight limit

Sports equipment on Wizz Air is capped at the same **32kg** ceiling as standard checked baggage, which gives plenty of room for a full set, shoes and wet-weather kit without coming close to the limit. There isn't a golf-specific dimension chart published — a standard travel cover for a full-size bag is accepted without issue.
What it costs (and why it isn't a fixed number)

This is the part worth being upfront about: reported prices for Wizz Air's sports equipment fee vary more than most, roughly **€55–€65 online depending on the route and how far ahead you book**, and around **€65 at the airport**. Older figures of €30–€40 still circulate online, but 2026 listings sit well above them. Wizz Air's pricing model adjusts by route, demand and how close to departure you are — the same golf bag fee can genuinely cost more on a busy August Faro flight than a quiet October one. Don't anchor on a single figure from a forum post; check the actual price shown for your dates when you book.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

Sports equipment needs to be added at least 3 hours before departure through your WIZZ account, but Wizz Air itself flags that space for it is limited on each flight — so booking it when you first book your flights, rather than closer to the date, avoids both a higher price and the risk of it not being available at all.
The alternative: skip the guesswork and rent at Faro

If you'd rather not gamble on which end of that price range you land on, renting removes the question entirely. Two operators run pickup points directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)**, one in the arrivals hall and one at a departures-terminal counter — you land, collect a set (or have one delivered to your hotel or first course), and there's no dynamic fee to track down in the first place.

Different operators offer different rates and delivery areas, so it's worth a quick comparison — our [full list of club rental shops in the Algarve](/shops) covers all of them, not just the two based at the airport.
Bottom line

Wizz Air will carry your golf clubs without issue as long as you book the sports equipment slot early and keep the bag under 32kg — the real thing to plan around is the price itself, which moves more than it does on other airlines. Book it the moment you book your flights to get the best shot at the lower end of that range, or sidestep it completely by renting once you're in Faro.

excerpt: Aer Lingus carries golf clubs free in Business class, but Economy pays a separate fee each way. Here's the difference and what Economy passengers can expect to pay.

content.text: Aer Lingus flies into Faro from Cork and Dublin, making it the natural choice for Irish golfers heading to the Algarve. It's also got a genuinely different rule from most of this series: which cabin you're sitting in changes whether you pay for your clubs at all.
How Aer Lingus treats golf clubs by cabin

Fly **Business class** and sports equipment, golf clubs included, is carried **free of charge** — no separate fee at all. Fly **Economy**, and it's charged as its own item, the same structure as most low-cost carriers: booked in advance, with a lower online rate and a higher one if you leave it for the airport.
Weight and quantity limits

The allowance is **23kg** per bag, and Aer Lingus limits you to **one piece of sports equipment per passenger** — so a second bag, or a set that's heavier than the norm, needs sorting separately rather than assumed to fit. Go over 23kg and standard excess baggage rates apply to the difference.
What Economy passengers pay

For Economy, golf clubs typically run at around **€40 per bag, per flight, booked online in advance**, rising to roughly **€50 if arranged through the reservations centre or at the airport** on the day. That's per direction, so a return trip means paying it twice unless you're flying Business both ways. As always, treat this as a guide figure and check the live price when you book, since it can vary by route and season.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

Add sports equipment online when you book or through Manage Booking ahead of departure — always the cheaper route compared to sorting it by phone or at the airport desk. If you're travelling as a group of golfers on one of Aer Lingus Regional's smaller aircraft, it's worth contacting them directly in advance, since those flights cap the total number of golf bags allowed on board.
The alternative: rent clubs right at Faro Airport

If you're flying Economy and the return fee starts to add up — or you'd simply rather not manage a golf bag through Cork or Dublin airport and back — renting on arrival is a straightforward alternative. Two operators are based directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)**, one in the arrivals hall and one at a departures-terminal counter, so you can pick up a set the moment you land or have one waiting at your hotel or first course.
For a broader comparison of rates and delivery areas, see our [full list of club rental shops in the Algarve](/shops).
Bottom line

If you happen to be flying Aer Lingus Business class, bringing your own clubs to the Algarve costs nothing extra — worth factoring in if you're weighing up the cabin upgrade. In Economy, budget somewhere around €80 return for the fee alone, and decide whether that's worth it compared to renting a set once you're in Faro.

excerpt: What Jet2 charges to fly with golf clubs to Faro, its 22kg allowance, and why pre-booking matters more here than with other airlines.

content.text: Jet2 flies a huge number of golfers into Faro every year, and if you're bringing your own clubs rather than renting, there's one detail that catches people out more with Jet2 than with other airlines: **pre-booking isn't just cheaper, it's expected**. Here's how Jet2 handles golf clubs, what it costs, and why booking early matters more here than it does with some other carriers.
How Jet2 classifies golf clubs

Golf clubs travel with Jet2 as **sports equipment**, in the hold only — there's no cabin option for a golf bag. It's booked and paid for as its own item, separate from your normal checked suitcase, so it doesn't eat into or share weight with your regular hold luggage allowance.
Weight limits

Jet2's golf allowance covers bags up to **22kg**, slightly more generous than the 20kg most other low-cost carriers allow, which gives a bit more breathing room for a full set plus shoes and extras. Go over that and you're charged an excess rate of roughly **£12 per kilo** on top. As always, weighing the bag before you leave home is worth the two minutes it takes.
What it costs — and why booking early actually matters

Jet2 lists sports equipment, golf clubs included, **from £35 when added online**, with the exact fee for your flight shown as you book — cheaper than adding them later. Prices can vary by route and season, so treat this as a guide figure and check the exact cost shown when you book.

The bigger point with Jet2 specifically: sports equipment space is limited on each flight, and **golf routes into the Algarve are exactly the kind of route that can sell out in peak summer**. Jet2 recommends booking golf clubs at the same time as your flights rather than leaving it until later — if you wait, you're not just risking a higher price, you're risking the airline not being able to fit your clubs on that flight at all.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

Add sports equipment during the initial flight booking, or afterwards through **Manage My Booking** on the Jet2 website or app — do this as early as possible rather than waiting for departure week, for the reason above. If you booked through a travel agent or as part of a Jet2holidays package, ask them to add it at the same time rather than sorting it separately later. Use a solid padded or hard-shell travel cover — hold luggage gets thrown around, and a thin cover won't stop a shaft bending or a driver head cracking in transit.
The alternative: rent clubs right at Faro Airport

Between the pre-booking pressure and paying the fee on both legs, quite a few Jet2 passengers heading to the Algarve decide it isn't worth the hassle and rent when they arrive instead. Two rental operators are based right at **Faro Airport (FAO)** — one with a desk in arrivals, another at a departures-terminal counter — so you can walk off the plane and either carry a set out with you or have it sent ahead to your hotel or first round.

Worth a look before you commit either way: our [club rental shops](/shops) page covers every rental operator across the Algarve, airport-based or not, with what each one charges and where they'll deliver to.
Bottom line

Jet2 isn't a difficult airline to fly with your own set, but it does punish leaving things late — book the sports equipment slot when you book the flights, not the week before, and you'll pay less and avoid any risk of it not fitting on the plane. If that timing pressure puts you off, renting on arrival at Faro sidesteps the whole issue.

excerpt: The golf club rental companies that pick up and drop off right at Faro Airport (FAO) — where to find each one, what they stock, roughly what it costs, and how to book before you fly.

content.text: Flying to the Algarve for golf and wondering whether to bring your own set? Hiring golf clubs at Faro Airport is the alternative most visiting golfers end up choosing for a short trip. Several rental companies operate directly from the terminal or deliver to it, so you can step off the plane, collect a bag, and be on the first tee without ever checking a golf travel case. This guide covers each option that works out of Faro Airport (FAO): where you collect the clubs, what they stock, roughly what it costs, and how to book before you fly.
Why hire clubs instead of flying with your own

Most airlines flying into Faro charge separately for golf clubs. Online, expect roughly £35–£45 or €40–€45 each way on Jet2, Ryanair, easyJet, Aer Lingus and TAP, and more on some others, such as around €80 each way on Lufthansa unless clubs are part of your allowance. Over a return trip for two people that adds up quickly, before you factor in the risk of damage in the hold or a bag that misses a connection. Hiring locally removes the fee and the bulky travel cover. The trade-off is that you play a set you are not used to, which matters more to low handicappers than to the average holiday golfer. For a longer stay, or if you are very particular about your clubs, flying with them can still be worth it.

For the exact golf-bag fees by carrier, see our guides to flying with clubs on [Ryanair](/guide/ryanair-golf-clubs-what-it-costs-to-fly-with-your-own-set-to-the-algarve), [easyJet](/guide/golf-clubs-on-easyjet-rules-sizes-and-what-it-actually-costs) and [Jet2](/guide/jet2-golf-clubs-fees-weight-limits-and-why-you-shouldn-t-leave-booking-late).
How club hire at Faro Airport works

The process is similar with each company. You book before you travel, then either collect at the airport or arrange delivery where it is offered. A typical bag includes a driver, irons, a wedge, a putter and a carry bag, but the exact contents vary, so check what is included when you book. Ladies' and left-handed sets are widely offered, while junior sets are less common. You normally return the clubs to the same place before your flight home.
Where to hire golf clubs at Faro Airport
Three rental companies offer collection at Faro Airport. ClubsToHire and MyCaddyMaster also offer delivery. Faro Golf Club Hire's website doesn't mention delivery, so ask if you need it.

content.note: Checked on company websites in November 2026. Prices can change, so confirm when you book.
content.caption: Golf club hire at Faro Airport compared

content.text: ClubsToHire

Pickup is at its shop in the **arrivals hall**, so you can collect your clubs as soon as you land. It is open from 07:00 to 23:00 for pre-booked times, with out-of-hours collection from 05:30 to 07:00 and from 23:00 to 00:30 for an extra €25. Sets include Callaway, TaylorMade, PXG, Cobra and Ping, with men's, ladies' and left-handed options. The company's headline price is from €50 per set per week, but that is not specific to Faro, so confirm your price when you book. It also delivers to hotels, resorts, villas and courses across the Algarve, and charges may apply depending on your location.
MyCaddyMaster

MyCaddyMaster uses a meeting point at the airport, which has been listed as **Cafe PAUL in the departures terminal**, so check your booking confirmation. Its sets come in three packs: Evolution, Performance and Excellence. The website headline says from €5 a day, while the set prices it lists run from €9.30 to €21.80, so enter your dates to see the exact price. Brands include Callaway, TaylorMade, Srixon, Cleveland, Cobra, XXIO and Ping, and men's, ladies', junior and left-handed sets are offered. Clubs can also be delivered to the place of your choice.
Faro Golf Club Hire

Faro Golf Club Hire offers collection at Faro Airport, with Ben Sayers, Callaway, Ping and TaylorMade sets, and options for men and women and for right- and left-handed players. Its website doesn't publish prices or delivery details, so phone for a quote and to confirm the arrangements.
What it costs

Prices depend on the company, the set and how long you hire for. At the airport, MyCaddyMaster lists sets from €9.30 to €21.80, ClubsToHire advertises from €50 a week across its locations, and Faro Golf Club Hire gives quotes on request. Elsewhere in the Algarve, shops that publish prices charge from €25 to €40 for one day and about €60 to €80 for a week. Compare that with around €80 return to fly a golf bag on Ryanair or about £84 on easyJet. Hiring for a week often costs about the same as flying with your own clubs, and sometimes less. Check the live price and any delivery charge when you book.
Booking and what to check before you fly

Book at least a few days ahead in peak season — spring and October — when fleets do sell out. Have your flight number ready so the pickup can be matched to your landing time, and flag straight away if you need a left-handed, ladies or junior set, or a particular driver loft or shaft flex. Confirm exactly where you are meeting the representative — arrivals hall, a named counter, or kerbside — and what happens if your flight is delayed. Check whether a trolley or push cart is included or extra, since most Algarve courses allow buggies and trolleys but few include them in the green fee. Finally, keep the booking confirmation on your phone; you will usually need to show it on collection.
If you would rather not deal with the airport at all

Airport pickup is convenient, but it is not the only way. Several Algarve rental shops deliver a set straight to your hotel or have it waiting at your first course, then collect it when you are done, so the clubs never touch the airport. Our [golf club rental](/club-rental) page lists providers across the region, including which areas each one delivers to, and the wider [golf shops](/shops) directory covers places that also handle repairs, fittings and sales if you are thinking of buying while you are here.
Bottom line

For a trip of a week or less, hiring clubs at Faro Airport is often the simpler choice, and it can also be cheaper: there is no travel cover to carry, no sports-equipment fee each way and no risk of damage in the hold. ClubsToHire is the easiest to reach on arrival, and MyCaddyMaster has a wide range of sets, including junior options. If you don't need to collect at the airport, our [golf club hire comparison](/club-rental) includes companies that deliver to your accommodation.

excerpt: Eurowings charges a flat, predictable fee for golf clubs rather than a confusing online-vs-airport split. Here's what it costs and how the allowance works.

content.text: Eurowings connects Faro to several German cities — Berlin, Cologne/Bonn, Düsseldorf, Hamburg and Stuttgart, plus Hannover in season — so it's mainly relevant if you're flying from Germany rather than the UK. Compared to the rest of this series, its golf clubs policy is refreshingly simple: there's no online-versus-airport pricing gap to worry about, just one flat fee.
How Eurowings classifies golf clubs

Golf equipment is accepted as checked baggage, but it's booked and charged as its own item — it doesn't count toward your normal checked bag allowance, so a golf bag is on top of any suitcase you're also bringing, not a substitute for it. You register it ahead of time through the Eurowings website when you book or via Manage Booking afterwards.
Weight and size limits

The allowance is a generous **32kg**, with combined dimensions (length + width + height) up to **158cm** — enough room for a full set, shoes and extras without needing to think too hard about what you pack.
What it costs

Eurowings prices golf equipment at roughly **€50 per flight segment** as a starting point, with the exact figure shifting a bit by route and flight length. Unlike Ryanair, easyJet or Jet2, there doesn't appear to be a clear discount for booking online well in advance versus adding it later — the fee is comparatively flat, which makes it easier to budget for even if it isn't necessarily the cheapest on this list. As always, confirm the current price for your specific flights when you book, since airline ancillary pricing changes.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

Register your golf equipment on eurowings.com during booking or afterwards via Manage Booking, ideally well before departure rather than at the airport. Pack it in a solid case — with a 32kg allowance there's little excuse for an under-protected bag, and hold luggage handling doesn't get any gentler just because the fee was straightforward.
The alternative: rent clubs right at Faro Airport

A flat, predictable fee is one thing, but it's still a fee each way, plus a golf bag to manage through two airports. Renting removes both. Two operators are based directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)** — one with a desk in the arrivals hall, another at a departures-terminal counter — so you can land, collect a set, and either use it straight away or have it sent ahead to your hotel or first course.
To see rates and delivery areas beyond just these two, check our [directory of club rental shops across the Algarve](/shops).
Bottom line

Eurowings makes the golf clubs decision easy to plan around, at least — a predictable flat fee and a generous 32kg allowance, with no timing games to play to get a better rate. Whether that's worth roughly €100 for a return trip, once you count both legs, comes down to how much you'd rather just rent and skip the extra bag altogether.

excerpt: Vueling's golf clubs fee runs higher than Ryanair or easyJet's, even with a more generous 32kg allowance. Here's what to expect if you're flying via Spain.

content.text: Vueling is more of a Spain-based option than a typical UK route into Faro — it's most useful if you're flying from Spain itself or connecting through Barcelona on your way to the Algarve. If that's your route, it's worth going in knowing that Vueling's golf clubs fee runs noticeably higher than what Ryanair or easyJet charge, so the maths on bringing your own set changes a bit.
How Vueling classifies golf clubs

Golf clubs travel under Vueling's **"Special Luggage"** category, which also covers things like skis and bikes. Like the low-cost carriers, it's a separate purchase from your normal checked bag — not something that can share or be pooled with a suitcase's weight allowance — and it has to be booked as its own item rather than assumed to be covered.
Weight limits

Vueling allows up to **32kg** for special luggage, noticeably more generous than the 20kg cap on Ryanair and easyJet or the 22kg on Jet2. In practice that's more headroom than most golfers will ever use — a full set with balls, shoes and wet-weather gear rarely gets close to 32kg — but it does mean less to worry about if you're packing heavier or travelling with extra kit.
What it costs

This is where Vueling stands out from the UK budget carriers: golf clubs typically run somewhere around **€45–€65 per item, per one-way flight, booked online**, and more again if you leave it for the airport. That's a higher starting price than Ryanair's €40 online. As always, Vueling prices special luggage by route and demand, so check the exact figure for your specific flights rather than relying on a general range.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

Add Special Luggage either during your original booking or afterwards through the Vueling website or app — always cheaper than adding it at the airport. At check-in, golf bags go through the **oversize luggage area** rather than a standard bag drop, and Vueling asks that the bag be properly packed, labelled and protected, since a loosely wrapped set is more likely to arrive with a bent shaft or a cracked head.
The alternative: rent at Faro and skip the higher fee entirely

Given Vueling's fee already sits above what most other airlines on this list charge, it's often the easiest case for renting instead of a hard decision. Two operators run pickup points directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)** — one in the arrivals hall, one at a departures-terminal counter — so you land, collect a set (or have one sent to your hotel or first course), and never touch the special luggage fee at all.
For a wider comparison of rates and delivery areas beyond just these two, our [club rental directory for the Algarve](/shops) lists rental operators across the region.
Bottom line

Vueling will take your golf clubs without any fuss — the 32kg allowance is generous and the process is straightforward — but the fee itself is one of the higher ones on this route, especially on a return trip once you've paid it twice. If you're already flying Vueling via Spain, it's worth weighing that cost against simply renting a set once you land in Faro.

excerpt: Transavia's golf clubs policy is stricter than most: a 15kg limit and an expectation that you register your clubs in advance. Here's what to know before you fly.

content.text: Transavia isn't a UK carrier — it flies into Faro from Amsterdam, Brussels, Eindhoven, Rotterdam and Paris-Orly, with some seasonal French routes on top — so this one's really for golfers coming from the Netherlands, Belgium or France. It's also the airline on this list with the most old-fashioned process for golf clubs: several sources describe it as the one where you're expected to **call ahead and get space confirmed**, not just tick a box online.
How Transavia handles golf clubs

Golf equipment is accepted, but reporting consistently points to Transavia wanting **advance notice** to secure a spot for it — either when you book or by contacting them directly — rather than assuming you can turn up with a golf bag and check it in on the day. More than one source specifically warns that showing up without having arranged it beforehand risks being told there's no room for it. Given how much airline policies shift, it's worth confirming directly with Transavia when you book rather than leaving it to chance.
Weight and quantity limits

Transavia's golf allowance is tighter than any other airline in this series: **15kg**, covering a bag of up to 14 clubs plus one pair of golf shoes. Go over that and the extra kilos are charged at Transavia's standard hold luggage rate rather than a golf-specific excess fee. You can register up to **two golf bags per passenger**, useful if you're travelling as a pair and want to book both under one booking.
What it costs

Golf clubs with Transavia are priced from **€42 each way when booked online**, and from **€50 if you add them at the airport** — assuming there is still space, which isn't guaranteed. The emphasis is on getting the space confirmed in advance rather than on the €8 saving. Treat €42 as a starting price and confirm the exact figure when you book, since airline ancillary pricing changes often.
How to book it

Add golf equipment during the booking process on Transavia.com, or contact Transavia directly to register it if you've already booked — do this as early as you can rather than close to departure, given the emphasis on securing space in advance. Pack the clubs properly regardless: a 15kg allowance doesn't leave much room to argue about a damaged bag being someone else's fault.
The alternative: skip the phone call and rent at Faro instead

Between the 15kg ceiling, the advance-registration requirement, and the risk of being turned away if you didn't arrange it ahead of time, Transavia is arguably the airline on this list where renting locally makes the most sense. Two operators run pickup points directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)** — one in the arrivals hall, one at a departures-terminal counter — so there's no call to make, no weight limit to squeeze under, and no chance of your clubs being refused at check-in.
Want to compare more than just the two airport options? Our [directory of club rental shops across the Algarve](/shops) lists every operator, including which ones deliver to your hotel or course.
Bottom line

Flying Transavia with your own clubs is possible, but it takes more advance planning than most airlines on this route — book the space early, stay well under 15kg, and don't assume you can sort it at the airport counter. If that sounds like more hassle than a short golf trip warrants, renting once you land in Faro cuts all of it out.

excerpt: Lufthansa usually lets golf clubs travel within your normal baggage allowance — except on its cheapest Light fare. Here's how the fare rules work and what it costs if you don't qualify.

content.text: Lufthansa flies into Faro from Frankfurt and Munich, so it's really an option for golfers travelling from Germany or connecting through one of Lufthansa's hubs on a longer journey. Like British Airways and TAP, it doesn't automatically charge a flat golf fee the way the low-cost carriers do — whether you pay comes down to your fare type.
How Lufthansa treats golf clubs

A golf bag containing your clubs, balls and a pair of shoes is classed as **sports baggage**, and on most fares it simply **counts toward your existing free baggage allowance** rather than being charged as an extra. The exception is Lufthansa's cheapest **Economy Light** fare, which excludes sports baggage from its allowance entirely — on that fare, golf clubs are always an additional cost, not something you can fit inside what's already included.
Weight and size limits

The allowance covers up to **32kg**, with combined dimensions (length + width + height) up to **220cm** — the most generous size limit of any airline in this series, giving plenty of room even for an oversized travel case. Sports baggage needs to be registered at least **24 hours before departure**, so it's not something to leave until you're already at the airport.
What it costs if it isn't included

If you're on a Light fare, or your golf bag pushes you past what your fare already includes, Lufthansa charges by route zone rather than a flat number. On European routes — which covers a Frankfurt or Munich flight to Faro — that's typically around **€80 each way**. Rates step up steeply for longer-haul routes, which isn't relevant for a Faro trip but shows the fee is genuinely route-based rather than fixed. Confirm the live price when you book, since these figures shift.
A perk worth knowing about if you fly Lufthansa often

Lufthansa also carries golf equipment free for its top-tier frequent flyers — **HON Circle, Senator and Star Alliance Gold members** — though that perk doesn't apply on Light fares or on routes to the US and Canada. If you or someone in your group holds that status, it's worth checking before assuming the standard fee applies.
The alternative: rent clubs right at Faro Airport

Even when the clubs travel for free, there's still a golf bag to manage through check-in, security and — if you're connecting via a Lufthansa hub — a transfer as well. Renting sidesteps all of that. Two operators are based directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)**, one in the arrivals hall and one at a departures-terminal counter, so you can land with nothing to collect from oversize baggage and either take a rented set with you or have it delivered to your hotel or first course.
For more rental options beyond these two, browse our [full directory of club rental shops in the Algarve](/shops).
Bottom line

Check your fare before assuming Lufthansa will charge you for golf clubs — on most tickets they simply use up your existing baggage allowance, and it's only the cheapest Light fare where you're guaranteed to pay extra. Either way, if a connection through a German hub already sounds like enough to manage, renting once you're in Faro removes the golf bag from the equation entirely.

excerpt: A breakdown of easyJet's sports equipment fees and weight limits for golf clubs, and why the numbers might make you rethink packing your own set.

content.text: EasyJet is one of the biggest carriers flying into Faro, and if you're bringing your own set for a golf trip to the Algarve, the clubs need to be booked as their own item — separate from your normal hold bag, with their own size limit and their own fee. Here's what easyJet actually charges, how the booking works, and a cheaper alternative worth considering before you check a golf bag at all.
How EasyJet classifies golf clubs

EasyJet books golf clubs under **"small sports equipment"**, the same category as things like a single snowboard bag. You're limited to **one piece of sports equipment per passenger**, and it has to travel in the hold — there's no cabin option for a golf bag. It's added to your booking as its own paid item, not folded into your regular checked baggage.
Weight limits

The small sports equipment allowance covers up to **20kg**, which a standard golf bag with a full set, balls and shoes normally falls within. Go over that and easyJet charges an excess fee in bands — roughly **£12 (around €12) per extra 3kg** — so it's worth weighing the bag at home rather than finding out at check-in. easyJet's page doesn't publish a fixed maximum length/width/height for golf bags specifically, but a standard hard or soft golf travel case is accepted without issue.
What it costs

In 2026, golf clubs on easyJet cost around **£42 per item, per one-way flight, when added online in advance**, and around **£52 if you leave it and pay at the airport** instead. As with any airline, these fees can be adjusted or vary slightly by route and season, so it's worth double-checking the exact current price in the "Add sports equipment" section when you book or manage your flight.
That's per direction, so a return flight means paying the fee twice, and it's per passenger — a couple travelling with two golf bags pays it twice over as well.
It doesn't replace your normal checked bag

easyJet is explicit that sports equipment and regular hold luggage weight **can't be pooled** — your golf clubs are a separate purchase from your suitcase, not an allowance you can top up with spare kilos from elsewhere. If you're also checking a normal bag for clothes, that's on top of the golf clubs fee. Packing clothes and shoes into the pockets of a padded golf travel bag, and travelling with just that as your one hold item, is a common way golfers trim the total cost.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

You can add sports equipment when you first book, later through **Manage Bookings** on the easyJet website or app, or during online check-in — all of which get you the lower online rate. Adding it at the airport desk or over the phone costs more, so it's worth sorting before you travel rather than leaving it to departure morning. Use a proper padded or hard-shell travel cover: hold luggage gets handled roughly, and a thin bag cover won't protect the clubs from a bent shaft or a cracked driver head.
The alternative: rent clubs right at Faro Airport

easyJet's own rules already make this less appealing than it sounds — clubs are a separate purchase from your suitcase, with their own weight cap, on top of an outbound and a return fee. So instead, a growing number of golfers flying easyJet into Faro just rent when they land. Two operators are set up right inside **Faro Airport (FAO)**: one in the arrivals hall, one at a departures-terminal counter. Grab a set on the spot, or have it dropped at your hotel or first tee — either way, there's no bag to check and no shaft to worry about bending in the hold.

Prices and delivery areas vary by operator, so it's worth a quick look at our [full list of club rental shops](/shops) across the Algarve before deciding — not every one of them is airport-based, and some cover specific towns more cheaply.
Bottom line

There's nothing complicated about bringing your own set on easyJet — book the sports equipment fee online ahead of time, stay under 20kg, and travel with a decent case. It's the maths that tends to change people's minds: two flights' worth of fees plus the small risk of damage, against a rental set waiting for you the moment you land.

excerpt: TUI Airways won't let you add golf clubs online — it has to be booked by phone, with limited space per flight. Here's what it costs for a Faro flight and why timing matters.

content.text: TUI Airways flies into Faro from Cardiff and, seasonally, East Midlands, and a lot of golfers book it as part of a wider TUI package holiday rather than a standalone flight. That package-holiday setup shows up in how golf clubs get booked too — this is the one airline in the series where you can't just tick a box during online checkout.
How TUI handles golf clubs

Sports equipment, golf clubs included, has to be **pre-booked by phone** with TUI rather than added through the normal online booking flow. Reports are consistent that space for it on each flight is genuinely limited, and that turning up without having pre-booked risks the equipment being refused at check-in. If you've booked through a TUI package holiday, your travel agent may be able to sort it for you at the same time — otherwise, look up TUI's current baggage/sports equipment contact line on their official site and call as early as you can, since numbers and processes do change.
What it costs

TUI prices sports equipment by destination band rather than a single flat fee. For **Portugal** specifically — which covers a Faro flight — reported pricing sits at around **£27 per one-way flight**, on the cheaper end of TUI's bands (longer routes and some other destinations cost more). That means budgeting roughly £54 for the fee alone on a return trip. Treat that figure as a guide and confirm the current price when you call to book, since TUI's bands and rates can shift.
Why booking early matters more here than usual

Between the phone-only booking process and genuinely limited space per flight, TUI is one of the least forgiving airlines on this list if you leave it late. Call as soon as you've got your flight or holiday booked, not the week before you travel — if the equipment allocation on your specific flight is already full, no amount of money fixes that at the airport.
The alternative: skip the phone call and rent at Faro

Given you already have to make a phone call and hope there's room, plenty of TUI passengers decide it's simpler to travel without clubs at all and rent once they land. Two operators are based directly inside **Faro Airport (FAO)** — one in the arrivals hall, one at a departures-terminal counter — so there's no call to make and no allocation to run out of. Collect a set the moment you land, or have one delivered to your hotel or first course.
Curious what else is out there beyond the airport options? Our [Algarve club rental directory](/shops) lists every operator, with rates and delivery areas.
Bottom line

TUI's fee for golf clubs to Portugal is actually one of the more affordable ones on this list — it's the process around it that's the sticking point. Call well ahead to lock in space, or sidestep the whole thing by renting once you're in Faro.

excerpt: Eight Algarve golf courses that genuinely suit beginners, checked against handicap rules, golfer feedback and practice facilities, from par-3 nines to forgiving 18-hole courses.

content.text: Taking up golf and planning a first trip south? The Algarve is one of the friendliest places in Europe to learn, but with nearly 40 courses to choose from, it is hard to tell which ones will genuinely welcome a new player. This guide picks the 8 best Algarve golf courses for beginners: four short nine-hole courses, three of which ask for no handicap at all, for your very first rounds, and four forgiving 18-hole courses to step up to once you can get the ball airborne.

The list is deliberately short. We only included courses where the evidence clearly points the same way, and left out several that often appear on beginner lists but play too tight, too hilly or too close to water for a new golfer. A course missing from this list isn't necessarily unsuitable, though: for some, we simply couldn't find enough evidence.
How we chose these courses
Every course here had to pass four checks:

**Access.** It either asks for no handicap at all, or for a handicap certificate a newer golfer can realistically have, usually a maximum of 28 for men and 36 for ladies. We checked this against each club's own rules, and where a club does not publish a limit, we say so.

**A forgiving layout.** Golfers who have played it consistently describe it as forgiving, open or well suited to higher handicaps, and at least one independent golf guide or local teaching professional says the same.
**No red flags.** We dropped any course where several players warned that it punishes wayward shots, is full of blind tee shots or forces long carries over water.
**Somewhere to practise.** The 18-hole courses all have a driving range or golf academy on site, so you can warm up or take a lesson before you play.
Do you need a handicap certificate to play golf in the Algarve?

Almost every 18-hole course in the Algarve asks for an official handicap, usually a maximum of **28 for men and 36 for ladies**. [Gramacho](/courses/gramacho) is slightly stricter at 27 and 35. How strictly this is checked varies, but the safe approach is to assume you will be asked, be honest when you book and keep pace with the group in front.

Short courses are different. Penina's nine-hole Resort Course states that no handicap is required, Vale de Milho does not ask for one, and Pine Cliffs' local rules let players without a handicap play, as long as they use the red tees. Balaia is the exception: the resort's guest information says a handicap is required, without giving a limit, so check with the club before you book.
The 8 best Algarve golf courses for beginners
1. Vale de Milho, Carvoeiro

A nine-hole, all par-3 course on the hillside above Carvoeiro, under a kilometre long in total, with the shortest hole just 70 metres. No handicap certificate is needed, although you should know basic golf etiquette, and the resident PGA professional gives lessons for all abilities. Clubs and trolleys can be hired, and nine holes cost €22 on the club's current price list. It is the gentlest introduction to a real course in the western Algarve.
2. Penina Resort Course, Portimão

The nine-hole Resort Course at the Penina Hotel & Golf Resort, designed by Sir Henry Cotton alongside the famous Championship course. It is a par 35 of 2,629 metres from the yellow tees, and Penina states plainly that no handicap is required. Players describe it as flat and beginner-friendly, and it is one of the most affordable ways to play a full-size Algarve course rather than a par-3 loop.
3. Pine Cliffs, Albufeira

A nine-hole clifftop course at Olhos de Água that the resort describes as perfect for beginners and advanced players alike, with a golf academy run by PGA instructors. The club's local rules let players without a handicap onto the course, as long as they play from the red tees. Most holes are short par 4s and par 3s. The exception is the sixth, the Devil's Parlour, a par 3 that the club describes as a 197-metre carry over a ravine, so ask the starter how to play it.
4. Balaia Golf Village, Albufeira

An all par-3 nine set in the grounds of the Balaia resort near Albufeira, with holes from roughly 67 to 160 metres. Turismo de Portugal describes it as ideal for beginners, and there is a practice range next to the clubhouse for warming up first. The club's 2025-26 price list puts a visitor's day green fee at €50. Note that the resort's guest information says a handicap is required, without giving a limit, so check with the club before you book if you have only just started playing.
5. Vilamoura Millennium, Vilamoura

When you are ready for 18 holes, Millennium is the most forgiving of Vilamoura's five courses. It is flat and easy to walk, and the back nine in particular is wide and open, so a slightly wayward drive rarely costs a ball. The front nine is tighter and tree-lined, so take your time there. Handicap limits are 28 for men and 36 for ladies. It is the most expensive course on this list, so look at the summer and twilight rates.
6. Morgado, Portimão

A wide, open course in the valley between Portimão and Monchique, and one that golfers regularly recommend to mid and high handicappers on holiday. The fairways are generous and there is little rough, so the main thing to avoid is the bunkers. At almost 6,400 metres it is long from the back tees, so play from the front. There are two practice tees, two chipping greens and a golf academy on site. Most sources give a maximum handicap of 28 for men and 36 for ladies.
7. Gramacho, Carvoeiro

Part of the Pestana resort in Carvoeiro, and recommended for higher handicappers by local PGA professionals and golf guides alike. The layout is open, with plenty of short par 4s, and its unusual design of 18 holes, 27 greens and several tee positions lets the course play to your level. Pestana itself says it can be enjoyed by players with a higher handicap. Some fairways roll and a few tee shots are blind, so it is a small step up from Millennium and Morgado. Handicap limits are 27 for men and 35 for ladies.
8. Benamor, Tavira

A course near Tavira laid out from Sir Henry Cotton's original plans and completed after his death by Howard Swan, in the quieter eastern Algarve, and one of the shortest 18-hole courses in the region at about 5,500 metres from the white tees. Players describe it as a good shorter course for higher handicaps, and the relaxed atmosphere takes the pressure off. It is hilly in places with a few blind shots, so a buggy or electric trolley helps. You will need a handicap certificate, with limits of 28 for men and 36 for ladies.
Courses we left off this list

Some courses that often appear on beginner lists did not pass our checks. [Alto Golf](/courses/alto-golf) and [Espiche](/courses/espiche) are good courses, but golfers repeatedly describe tight, tree-lined or sloping fairways that punish a wayward shot. [Amendoeira O'Connor](/courses/amendoeira-oconnor) is more forgiving than its Faldo sister course, but its many lakes mean high handicappers can lose a lot of balls. [Vale da Pinta](/courses/vale-da-pinta) is better suited to low and mid handicaps. Save them for your second or third trip.
Tips for your first golf trip to the Algarve

**Rent clubs rather than flying with your own.** Almost every course offers rental sets, and it saves both the airline fee and the worry of damaged clubs while you are still deciding whether the game is for you.
**Book the first or last tee times of the day.** The course is quieter, the light is better, the temperature is kinder in summer, and you will not feel rushed.

**Travel in the low season if you can.** Green fees across the region drop in the summer and winter months, and courses around Tavira tend to be quieter than those around Vilamoura and Quinta do Lago.

**Play the forward tees and use ready golf.** Nobody minds a beginner who keeps up. Carry a few spare balls, hit when you are ready rather than waiting for strict order, and pick up once you have had enough on a hole.
Where to start

If you have barely swung a club, begin at [Vale de Milho](/courses/vale-de-milho), [Penina Resort](/courses/penina-resort) or [Pine Cliffs](/courses/pine-cliffs), none of which needs a handicap, and book a lesson; our guide to [golf lessons in the Algarve](/guide/golf-lessons-in-the-algarve) lists the academies. Once you are getting the ball airborne consistently, step up to [Millennium](/courses/vilamoura-millennium) or [Morgado](/courses/morgado) for your first full 18. Use the [course map](/) to compare handicap limits and locations, and check current green fees with the club before you book, as they change by season.

excerpt: Ryanair's current fees, weight limits and booking rules for checking golf clubs to Faro — and why renting on arrival is worth considering instead.

content.text: If you're flying into Faro with Ryanair for a golf trip to the Algarve, the first practical question is usually the most annoying one: what does it actually cost to bring your own clubs? Ryanair treats golf clubs as sports equipment rather than a normal checked bag, which means a separate fee, its own size and weight rules, and a booking step that's easy to miss if you leave it until the airport. Here's what to expect, and a cheaper alternative worth considering before you pack a golf bag at all.
How Ryanair classifies golf clubs

Golf clubs fall under Ryanair's **sports equipment** category, alongside things like skis and bicycles. They can't travel in the cabin — a golf bag is far too long and heavy for hand luggage — so they go in the hold, but as a distinct item from your checked suitcase, booked and paid for separately through the "Sports Equipment" option when you manage your booking.
Weight and size limits

Ryanair's general sports equipment allowance covers items up to **20kg**, and a full golf bag with a dozen-plus clubs, balls and shoes usually sits comfortably under that if it's your only hold item. If your bag comes in heavier, you're charged an excess baggage rate per kilo over the limit, so it's worth weighing it at home before you leave — bathroom scales and a hold-all strap work fine for this. Oversized or excessively heavy bags can also be refused at check-in, so don't assume a slightly-too-big travel cover will slide through.
What it costs

Ryanair's own fee table lists golf clubs at **£40 / €40 per item, per one-way flight, when booked online**, rising to **£50 / €50 if you add them at the airport**. Because the exact figure moves around, always check the current price in the "Sports Equipment" section when you book or manage your flight, rather than relying on a number from an old forum post.
That fee is per direction, so a return trip means paying it twice — once each way — and it's per item, so a second golf bag (if you're travelling as a couple, say) is charged again in full.
It doesn't replace your normal checked bag

Golf clubs are booked **in addition to** any regular hold luggage, not instead of it. If you're also checking a suitcase for clothes, that's a second fee on top. Some golfers get around this by packing clothes and shoes inside the golf bag itself (many travel covers have pockets big enough for it) and travelling with just the one hold item — worth considering if you're trying to keep costs down.
How to add golf clubs to your booking

Add sports equipment either when you first book the flight, or afterwards through **Manage My Booking** on the Ryanair website or app — this needs to be done up to a couple of hours before departure to get the online rate. Doing it at the airport desk is always the most expensive route and, on a busy departures morning, adds a queue you don't need. Once it's added, use a proper hard-shell or padded travel case: airline handlers aren't gentle with hold luggage, and a soft cover offers your clubs almost no protection against a rough throw onto a baggage cart.
The alternative: rent clubs right at Faro Airport

Once you add up the outbound fee, the return fee, and the risk of your clubs turning up dented or delayed, a lot of golfers travelling to the Algarve skip bringing their own set entirely. A few rental operators work directly out of **Faro Airport (FAO)** itself — you land, collect a set from the arrivals hall or a departures-terminal counter, and either take it with you or have it delivered to your hotel or first course. No golf bag to check, no sports equipment fee, and nothing to worry about damaging in transit.
If you'd rather compare more options first, our [club rental shops](/shops) page lists rental providers across the Algarve, including which ones deliver to your course or hotel.
Bottom line

Bringing your own clubs on Ryanair is straightforward as long as you book the sports equipment fee online in advance, keep the bag under 20kg, and pack it properly. Budget £80 return for the privilege once both legs are counted — then weigh that against a few days of local rental, which for many golfers ends up being the simpler and cheaper choice for a short Algarve trip.

excerpt: Both are western Algarve favourites near Lagos, but they test different parts of your game. Here's how the hillside Boavista and the tightly wooded Espiche actually compare.

content.text: Boavista and Espiche are the two courses golfers based around Lagos, in the western Algarve, end up choosing between. Both are well inland of the resort belt, both keep a lower profile than the Golden Triangle courses, and both are genuinely good — but they test very different parts of your game. Here's how they compare.
Two different tests above Lagos

Boavista, designed by **Howard Swan** and opened in 2002, climbs through cork-oak woodland on a hillside above Lagos, with genuine sea views on the higher holes and a slope rating of 138 — one of the tougher numbers in the western Algarve. Espiche, designed by South African architect **Peter Sauerman** and opened in 2012, sits inland in a protected nature reserve with views towards the Serra de Monchique, and plays to a gentler slope of 130. On paper Espiche looks like the easier round. In practice, plenty of golfers who've played both would disagree.
Boavista: hillside golf with a tough finish

At 6,167 metres par 71 from the back tees (5,747 m from the whites), Boavista splits into a resort nine that winds through the residential complex and a country nine that climbs into cork-oak terrain — and it's the closing stretch, including a pair of holes either side of a ravine, that golfers consistently flag as the real test. Fairways are generally wide and forgiving; the trouble comes from the elevation changes and what's waiting if you miss a green. It's also the more established of the two, with **184 reviews averaging 4.3 out of 5** in our own data.
Espiche: shorter on paper, unforgiving in practice

Espiche plays 5,890 metres par 72 through native Algarve scrub and vineyard views, and it's built to work with the natural contours of the land rather than against them — which sounds gentle until you miss a fairway. The rough either side of the fairways is genuinely penal: stray off line here and there's a real chance you won't find the ball, let alone hit a recovery shot. It's a course that rewards straight hitting far more than raw distance, and it's noticeably quieter than most Algarve courses, which regular players tend to rate as one of its biggest attractions.
Which one should you play?

If you want an established, well-rated course with sea views and a properly tough finish, play Boavista — its wider fairways make it the more forgiving tee-to-green test despite the higher slope rating. If you're a straight hitter who wants a quiet, scenic round and doesn't mind being punished for missing a fairway, Espiche is the better fit; just don't let the lower slope number fool you into leaving the driver on cruise control. Green fees start from **€65** at Espiche and **€74** at Boavista, so price is unlikely to decide it for you.
Where to stay

Boavista has its own on-site hotel, the 5-star [Boavista Golf & Spa Resort](https://www.booking.com/hotel/pt/boavista-golf-resort-spa.html), with a heated indoor pool, spa and tennis courts right next to the course. Espiche doesn't have an on-site hotel — most golfers playing it are staying in or around Lagos and driving out.

Want the numbers side by side instead? [Open the course comparator](/?compare=boavista,espiche) to see Boavista and Espiche's price, slope, handicap limits and facilities pulled straight from our live course data.

**How much will the trip cost?** See our guide to [how much a golf trip to Lagos and Portimão costs](/guide/how-much-does-a-golf-trip-to-lagos-and-portimao-cost) if you book it yourself, with month-by-month totals and example hotels.

excerpt: Two 18-hole courses at the same Silves resort, built by two major-winning designers in the same year. Here's how the desert-style Faldo Course and the water-laced O'Connor Course actually compare.

content.text: Amendoeira Golf Resort near Silves has two 18-hole courses built by two very different major-winning names, opened in the same year, sharing the same clubhouse and the same on-site hotel. They're often sold as a package, but they're not interchangeable rounds. Here's how the Faldo and O'Connor courses actually differ, and which one to book first.
Same resort, same year, two different designers

Both courses opened in 2008 — the Faldo Course during Portugal Masters week that year — and both share Amendoeira's clubhouse, driving range and practice facilities. But **Sir Nick Faldo** and **Christy O'Connor Jr.** built genuinely different golf. Faldo went desert-style: cacti and wild scrub stand in for rough, crushed limestone bunkers replace the usual Algarve sand, and the whole course has a rugged, reddish character unlike anything else in the region. O'Connor Jr. built something closer to traditional parkland, routed through a fertile valley with lakes in play on several holes.
The Faldo Course: Portugal's best, and it plays like it

At 6,598 metres par 72 from the back tees, the Faldo Course was named **Portugal's Best Golf Course** at the 2016 World Golf Awards, and it's still the one that shows up on "best of the Algarve" lists. It's a strategic course rather than a brutal one — Faldo built it around shot placement, so length off the tee matters less than picking the right line into firm, well-bunkered greens. Rocky outcrops and Mediterranean scrub line the fairways, and the course rewards patience more than power.
The O'Connor Course: greener, with more water to avoid

The O'Connor Jr. course plays 6,708 metres par 72 from its back tees through a greener, more traditional valley setting, with lakes woven through the round. Despite its reputation, it isn't the shorter course: from the back tees it's about 110 metres longer than the Faldo, and from the white tees the two are within 25 metres of each other (6,273 and 6,296 metres). It is generally considered the more forgiving of the two off the tee, which is why it tends to suit mid- and high-handicappers better than the Faldo — but the water hazards mean it still asks for precision on the approach, not just length.
Which one should you play?

If you want the course with the pedigree — the award, the desert-style design, the tougher strategic test — play the Faldo first. If you'd rather a greener round where the main thing to avoid is water rather than a wayward drive into scrub, start with the O'Connor. Both share the same maximum handicap (28 men, 36 ladies) and the same green fee from **€100**, so most golfers visiting Amendoeira simply play both across a trip.
Where to stay

Both courses share the same on-site hotel, [Amendoeira Golf Resort](/hotels/amendoeira-golf-resort), a 4-star property of self-catering apartments and villas with two outdoor pools, six tennis courts and two restaurants, set right inside the resort between the two courses. You can [book it directly on Booking.com](https://www.booking.com/hotel/pt/amendoeira-golf-resort.html).

Want the numbers side by side instead? [Open the course comparator](/?compare=amendoeira-faldo,amendoeira-oconnor) to see the Faldo and O'Connor's price, length, handicap limits and facilities pulled straight from our live course data.

**How much will the trip cost?** See our guide to [how much a golf trip to Albufeira costs](/guide/how-much-does-a-golf-trip-to-albufeira-cost) if you book it yourself, with month-by-month totals and example hotels.

excerpt: One put the Algarve on the golfing map in 1966; the other is a relaxed nine-hole loop across the road. Here's how Penina's two very different courses actually compare, honestly.

content.text: Both courses sit on the same Penina estate near Portimão and share the same hotel, but they're not really rivals — they're two completely different scales of golf. One is the course that put the Algarve on the golfing map. The other is a relaxed nine-hole loop across the road from it. Here's what each one actually offers.
The estate Sir Henry Cotton built

Three-time Open Champion **Sir Henry Cotton** transformed rice paddies into this 360-acre parkland estate, and the Championship Course he opened in 1966 was the first 18-hole golf course built in the Algarve — a genuinely historic claim, not a marketing one. The Resort Course came later as a shorter companion loop on the same grounds.
Championship: real history, mixed recent form

At 6,273 metres par 73, the Championship Course has hosted the Portuguese Open on multiple occasions, most recently in 2006, and its flat-but-deceptive routing through former rice paddies remains one of the most recognisable rounds in the region. Worth knowing before you book: player reviews over the past few years have flagged inconsistent fairway and green conditioning, alongside signs of renewed investment and improved upkeep more recently. It's still a course worth playing for the history alone — just go in with realistic expectations on turf condition rather than assuming five-star polish throughout.
Resort: a relaxed nine, playable as eighteen

The Resort Course plays nine holes at par 35 over 2,987 metres, or a full par-71 round of 5,964 metres by playing the same nine twice from different tees — the way most visitors actually play it. Bermuda 419 fairways and Creeping Bent greens keep it in decent shape, no handicap certificate is required, and the course holds Audubon Cooperative Sanctuary status for its wildlife management. It's a genuinely good option for beginners, families, or a fast evening round rather than a lesser version of the Championship course next door.
Which one should you play?

If you want the history, the tournament pedigree and a proper 18-hole test, play the Championship Course — just don't expect flawless conditioning on every visit. If you want a relaxed, inexpensive round with no handicap requirement, or you're introducing someone to golf, play the Resort Course. Green fees start from **€77** on the Championship and just **€28** on the Resort, and since they sit across the road from each other on the same estate, playing both is easy to arrange.
Where to stay

Both courses share the same on-site hotel, [Penina Hotel & Golf Resort](/hotels/penina-hotel), the Algarve's original five-star property, with six dining venues and direct access to both courses. You can [book it directly on Booking.com](https://www.booking.com/hotel/pt/penina-hotel-golf-resort.html).

Want the numbers side by side instead? [Open the course comparator](/?compare=penina-championship,penina-resort) to see the Championship and Resort courses' price, length, handicap limits and facilities pulled straight from our live course data.
